title: Form I-9 and E-Verify Employment Eligibility Compliance FAQs

body_markdown:
New-hire compliance is one of the few areas where HR leaders have almost no margin for error, and Form I-9 and E-Verify are consistently two of the most misunderstood parts of it. Many HR leaders are trying to keep policies current and support managers with compliant hiring decisions while also being asked to add compliance expertise without increasing headcount. Confusing these two requirements, or assuming one satisfies the other, is a common way that gap shows up. Asure works with HR leaders on exactly this kind of new-hire compliance question, and this FAQ walks through what Form I-9 and E-Verify actually require, where they overlap, and where employers commonly get the timing or the obligation wrong.


## Is Form I-9 required for every new hire


Yes. Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification, is legally required for every employer, for every employee hired to work in the United States, regardless of company size or the state the employer operates in. This requirement exists independently of E-Verify. An employer with one employee and an employer with thousands of employees carry the same underlying obligation to complete Form I-9 for each employee they hire to work in the U.S.


That obligation gets harder to execute consistently exactly as a company grows. More hiring managers, more locations, and faster onboarding all raise the odds that one manager handles the form differently than another, which is the specific gap Asure works with HR leaders to close.


The current Form I-9 edition is dated 01/20/25 and expires 05/31/2027. The prior 08/01/23 edition became unusable for new hires after July 31, 2026, so any employer still using that older version is out of compliance. Because USCIS periodically updates the form, HR teams should confirm they are using the current version posted on[uscis.gov](https://www.uscis.gov/i-9) rather than assuming a form already on file or downloaded previously is still current. (Current as of September 2026; confirm the current edition at uscis.gov/i-9 before each use. Refresh owner: Asure HR Compliance content team.)


## What is the difference between Form I-9 and E-Verify


Form I-9 is the underlying legal requirement. It requires the employer and the employee to complete a form and review specific documents establishing identity and work authorization within set timeframes around the hire date.


E-Verify is a separate, internet-based system that takes the information already collected on Form I-9 and electronically cross-checks it against federal records, according to[E-Verify.gov](https://www.e-verify.gov/about-e-verify/what-e-verify-is) . E-Verify does not stand in for Form I-9. It works from the I-9 data, which means Form I-9 has to be completed correctly first, whether or not the employer also uses E-Verify.


## Is E-Verify mandatory for every employer


No. Under federal law, E-Verify is not mandatory for most private employers. Where it becomes mandatory federally is for federal contractors and subcontractors that fall under the federal contractor E-Verify clause, as documented by[E-Verify.gov](https://www.e-verify.gov/employers/enrolling-in-e-verify/federal-contractors) . Under FAR 22.1803, that clause applies to federal contracts exceeding $150,000, and flows down to subcontracts above $3,500, so not every federal subcontractor is automatically covered. Outside of that federal contractor rule, most private employers can choose whether to enroll in E-Verify, unless a state law says otherwise, which is the next question.


## Do any states require E-Verify beyond the federal contractor rule


Yes, and this is where HR leaders most often get tripped up, because the federal contractor rule is not the only path to a mandatory E-Verify obligation. A number of states require E-Verify for most or all private employers under state law, independent of whether that employer holds a federal contract.


The specific list of states, and the employee-count thresholds some of them apply, change over time, so a fixed list here would go stale. Rather than rely on a point-in-time snapshot, HR leaders should check their state's current requirement directly at[everify.uscis.gov](https://everify.uscis.gov/) (E-Verify account access has moved there and is migrating to Login.gov) before assuming state law doesn't apply to them. It's also worth knowing that the system itself can go dark. E-Verify was unavailable during the October 2025 federal government shutdown, and USCIS tolled the standard three-business-day case-creation window for the days it was down, so employers with cases in progress during any future outage should watch for similar tolling guidance rather than assume normal deadlines still apply.


## Does using E-Verify remove the need to complete Form I-9


No. This is one of the most consequential misunderstandings in new-hire compliance. E-Verify runs on top of Form I-9 data, it does not replace the form or the underlying legal obligation to complete it. An employer enrolled in E-Verify, whether by choice, by a federal contract, or by state mandate, still has to complete Form I-9 for every new hire, on the same timeline, with the same documentation review, as an employer that never touches E-Verify at all.


## What happens if a company gets Form I-9 or E-Verify wrong


Getting the timing, the documentation, or the applicable E-Verify obligation wrong carries real exposure. Form I-9 errors, whether missed deadlines, incomplete sections, or accepting the wrong combination of documents, can surface during a federal audit and trigger civil monetary penalties, in addition to the time and legal cost of responding to the audit itself. Getting E-Verify obligations wrong carries its own risk: an employer that is required to use E-Verify by a federal contract or a state mandate and fails to do so is out of compliance with that specific requirement, on top of any Form I-9 issues.


For an HR leader, the practical risk is less about any single mistake and more about consistency. New-hire volume, manager turnover, and multi-state hiring all make it easier for I-9 timing or state-specific E-Verify obligations to slip through inconsistently across locations or hiring managers. That's the exact failure pattern the onboarding workflow in AsureCentral and Asure HR Compliance are built to close, covered directly below.


## How can HR leaders keep I-9 timing and documentation consistent without adding headcount


This is the day-to-day version of the problem, and it is where most HR leaders actually feel the gap: not a lack of knowledge that Form I-9 matters, but a lack of a consistent process for making sure it happens correctly every time a manager makes a hire.


The HR and onboarding workflow in AsureCentral helps employers capture and organize Form I-9 documentation at the moment of hire, so the required verification steps are built into onboarding rather than handled as a separate, easy-to-forget task. For example, an HR leader managing hiring across several locations can use that onboarding workflow to standardize how new-hire documentation is collected and stored across every manager and every site, instead of relying on each location to remember the process independently.


## Where can HR leaders get help interpreting a state's E-Verify obligation


State E-Verify law is exactly the kind of question that does not come up often enough to justify a full-time compliance hire, but carries real risk when it is answered incorrectly. Asure HR Compliance gives HR leaders on-demand access to certified HR professionals who can help clarify whether a state E-Verify mandate applies, without hiring dedicated in-house compliance staff. That kind of support is built for exactly the situation described above: an HR leader who needs a reliable answer on a specific state's requirement and a place to route the question, rather than a generic compliance checklist.


## Getting Form I-9 and E-Verify right, without building an in-house compliance team


Form I-9 is a universal, non-negotiable requirement for every employer and every new hire. E-Verify is a narrower obligation that only some employers are required to carry, whether through a federal contract or a state law, and it never substitutes for the I-9 itself. Getting both right consistently, across managers, locations, and states, is an ongoing process question more than a one-time policy decision.
